items.content:
The car came in with a complaint that sounded simple at first.

The owner said the transmission warning light would come on once in a while, then disappear again before anyone could properly check it. The car still moved, it still drove, and from the outside nothing looked dramatic. No smoke, no rough noise, no obvious mechanical failure. Just that random warning showing up and leaving like it had a mind of its own.

Normally, that is the kind of issue many people would treat as a regular repair problem and stop there.

But this is where automotive cybersecurity and vehicle auditing become interesting.

Modern cars do not only fail mechanically. They also behave like networks. Different control modules are constantly talking to each other, checking status, sending updates, expecting replies, and making decisions based on what they hear on the bus.

So when a warning appears randomly, sometimes the real issue is hidden inside that communication.

I connected to the CAN network and started the way I always like to start by observing first.

No rush. No assumptions. Just watch the traffic and understand what normal looks like.

The terminal shows the interface came up properly, the bus was active, and traffic was flowing. From there, I watched the identifiers moving across the network and checked the diagnostic side as well.

On the surface, the car was talking normally.

But then the diagnostic result gave the first real clue.

U0101 – Lost Communication With TCM

At that point, the issue became clearer.

The Transmission Control Module was not staying consistently available on the network. Something was interrupting that communication. It may come back, disappear again, then return once more , and from the driver’s side, all they notice is a warning light that seems random.

Now, that does not automatically mean somebody hacked the car.

It could be a failing module, unstable power, damaged wiring, a connector issue, intermittent CAN communication, firmware problems, or another module causing interference on the bus.

But from an auditing perspective, it is still important because now you have evidence that one of the vehicle’s critical systems is not communicating consistently.

That is where the investigation really starts.

You begin checking when the module drops off, whether other ECUs are reporting communication problems, whether the issue happens under certain conditions, and whether the network behavior changes around the same time as the warning.

This is why automotive cybersecurity is interesting to me.

Sometimes the issue you see on the dashboard is only the surface.

The useful evidence is buried inside the vehicle’s network.

items.content:
RT @Itsfoss: Open source maintainers are complaining about a new kind of harassment: AI-generated spam at scale.

The QEMU virtualization project was hit hard when a single user filed 132 bug reports in under 10 minutes. 

Many were created seconds apart, none followed the bug report template, and not one showed any sign of human analysis or a proposed fix. Just raw AI output dumped into the tracker.

Red Hat's Daniel Berrangé, who maintains QEMU, called it

"a denial-of-service attack on maintainers". 

"Reports ignored the bug template and showed no sign of any human analysis," he wrote, pushing him to call on GitLab to implement rate limiting for non-members.

This is not an isolated event. Maintainers across GitHub and GitLab are describing the same pattern: AI tools make it so cheap to generate and submit that bad-faith or careless users can flood a project with junk in minutes. 

The people on the receiving end are mostly unpaid volunteers working to maintain open source projects in their spare time.

Some projects are now shutting down outside contributions entirely. Others are updating their contributor agreements to require human-written attestations. GitHub is reportedly building emergency tools to help.

In the meantime, maintainers can do nothing but complain.
